passages.happening:
‘In the eighth month of the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah, the son of Iddo’ (verse 1). The LORD was very angry with their fathers (verse 2). So the people are told what the LORD of Hosts says: ‘Return to Me, declares the LORD of Hosts, and I will return to you’ (verse 3).

They are not to be like their fathers, who heard the former prophets call them to turn from their evil ways and did not listen (verse 4). Where are their fathers now, and the prophets, do they live for ever (verse 5)? But God's words overtook their fathers, and they repented and said that the LORD had dealt with them as their ways deserved (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
The date is October or November 520 BC, two months after Haggai's first message. The temple's foundations had been laid years before, but the work had stopped, and Haggai had just stirred the people to begin again.

The book opens not with a vision but with a call to return, which frames everything after it. The former prophets were the prophets before the exile, Isaiah, Jeremiah and the rest, whose warnings the fathers ignored. The fathers died, and the prophets died too, but God's words did what they said. The exile itself proved the prophets right.

The promise is two-sided. God does not ask his people to come back to a God who is far off. If they return to him, he will return to them.
passages.later: Malachi uses the same words a century later: ‘Return to Me, and I will return to you’ (Malachi 3:7). Ezra names Zechariah with Haggai as the prophets who urged the rebuilding (Ezra 5:1).
passages.asks: God promises to return to those who return to him. Ask what returning to God would look like in your life now. And the former generation did not listen. Ask what warning you have been treating as old news.

passages.t: Horsemen among the myrtles, and four horns
passages.happening:
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, Zechariah sees in the night a man on a red horse standing among myrtle trees in a hollow, with red, sorrel and white horses behind him (verses 7-8). They have been sent to patrol the earth, and they report that the whole earth is at rest and quiet (verses 10-11). The angel of the LORD asks how long God will withhold mercy from Jerusalem, with which he has been angry for seventy years (verse 12). The LORD answers with kind and comforting words (verse 13): he is very jealous for Jerusalem and Zion, and fiercely angry with the nations at ease, ‘For I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity’ (verse 15). He will return to Jerusalem with mercy, and his house will be rebuilt (verse 16).

Then Zechariah sees four horns, the horns that scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem (verses 18-19), and four craftsmen who come to terrify them and throw them down (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The night visions came about February 519 BC. Myrtle was a low evergreen that grew in damp places. Horsemen patrolling the empire would call to mind the Persian royal riders who carried the king's messages along its roads.

The report that the earth is at rest is not good news. The empire is quiet, Darius has crushed the revolts, and nothing has changed for Jerusalem. Seventy years recalls Jeremiah's promise that the exile would last that long. Horns stand for power in the Bible, as the horns of a wild ox; the four horns are the nations that scattered God's people, and the four craftsmen are the powers God raises to bring them down.

The visions are symbolic scenes explained by an angel. What matters is the angel's explanation: God has not forgotten Jerusalem.
passages.later: Jeremiah had said the exile would last seventy years (Jeremiah 25:11-12). Isaiah too accused Babylon of going beyond what God intended: ‘You showed them no mercy’ (Isaiah 47:6).
passages.hard:
If God was only a little angry, why was the destruction of Jerusalem so terrible?

Verse 15 says God was a little angry, but the nations added to the calamity. It is a hard line to read after the horrors of the Babylonian siege. This does not mean that God took Judah's sin lightly; verses 2 to 6 insist that his anger was great and justified. It means that the nations used as his instruments went far beyond the judgment he intended, acting out of cruelty and ambition rather than justice. Isaiah makes a similar charge against Babylon and against Assyria. Interpreters differ on how far to press the word little: some take it as relative, brief anger compared with lasting mercy, as in Isaiah 54:7-8.

The verse gives no warrant to call any people's suffering in war, then or now, deserved.
passages.asks: The empire was at rest while Jerusalem lay in ruins. Ask where your own comfort has made you stop asking God how long. And God answers with kind and comforting words. Ask what comfort you need to hear from him.
